# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Clubhead speed at impact is the dominant controllable determinant of drive
distance, and the golf downswing is one of the most-studied examples of a
*sequenced* multi-segment rotation in sport biomechanics
[@hume2005; @mcphee2022]. Across measurement systems and populations, the
downswing of a skilled golfer shows a characteristic order: the pelvis
reaches its peak angular speed first, then the thorax, then the lead arm,
and finally the club, with each successive segment reaching a higher peak
speed than the one before it [@cheetham2008; @tinmark2010]. This pattern —
the *kinematic sequence*, an instance of the general proximal-to-distal
(P→D) sequencing observed in throwing and striking skills
[@putnam1993] — is routinely interpreted as the visible signature of
mechanical energy being generated in the large proximal segments and
transferred outward to the small, fast distal ones.

That interpretation immediately raises a question that the descriptive
literature does not settle:

> **Should a golfer attempt to transfer energy from proximal to distal
> segments *early* in the downswing, or should energy be *retained* in the
> proximal segments early and the transfer deliberately *accelerated* late?**

The question is not academic. The two strategies imply opposite coaching
cues (e.g., "fire the club from the top" versus "hold the lag and let it
release"), opposite torque programs at the wrists and torso, and different
predictions for what counterfactual decompositions of a measured swing
should show. It also connects to a long-standing puzzle in the modeling
literature: simple double-pendulum analyses have argued since the 1960s that
the highest clubhead speeds arise when the distal joint is *not* driven
early — indeed when the release of the club is passively or actively
delayed [@cochran1968; @jorgensen1970; @milburn1982; @pickering1999] —
while the coaching translation of the kinematic sequence often emphasizes
initiating distal motion promptly after transition.

The UpstreamDrift project approaches this question with *counterfactual
dynamics*. Two decompositions are implemented across its physics engines:

- the **zero-torque counterfactual (ZTCF)** — the acceleration the system
  would exhibit at the current instant if all applied joint torques were
  removed, isolating what accumulated motion, gravity, and inter-segment
  coupling produce on their own; and
- the **zero-velocity counterfactual (ZVCF)** — the acceleration the
  applied torques would produce at the current pose if the system were
  momentarily at rest, isolating instantaneous muscular effort from
  motion-dependent effects.

Preliminary ZTCF/ZVCF analyses conducted with the repository's MATLAB
pipeline (see @sec-ztcf) motivated the hypothesis examined in this article:
that *restraining* the P→D handoff early in the downswing — keeping kinetic
energy in the proximal segments and in the arms-plus-club system rotating as
a quasi-rigid unit — and accelerating the handoff late, may be the more
effective strategy. This article evaluates that hypothesis against the
published literature and specifies how it can be tested quantitatively with
the tools already present in the repository.

**Contributions.** The article makes five contributions:

1. a synthesis of the mechanics of sequenced swings, from the summation-of-speed
   principle to segment-interaction dynamics and parametric energy transfer
   (@sec-mechanics);
2. a methodological account of what "energy transfer" means operationally —
   joint power, joint-force power, segmental energy accounting, and induced
   accelerations (@sec-energyflow);
3. a critical review of the empirical evidence on where P→D transfer occurs
   and how it differs between skilled and less-skilled players
   (@sec-evidence);
4. a formalization of the early-versus-late transfer question, including
   the ZTCF/ZVCF counterfactual framework and the specific predictions the
   "retain-early / release-late" hypothesis makes (@sec-timing,
   @sec-ztcf); and
5. an inventory of the models and computations available in UpstreamDrift
   today, an honest gap analysis, and a set of falsifiable simulation
   experiments that would decide the question (@sec-repo,
   @sec-proposed-experiments).

# Mechanics of sequenced swings {#sec-mechanics}

## The summation-of-speed principle and its limits {#sec-summation}

The oldest formalization of P→D sequencing is the *summation of speed*
principle: in skills demanding high end-point speed, each segment should
begin its motion at the moment of peak speed of the segment proximal to it,
so that distal speed is "built on top of" proximal speed [@bunn1972].
Milburn applied the principle directly to golf with a double-pendulum
analysis of the downswing and found the characteristic pattern of an
initially dominant proximal (arm) rotation followed by rapid distal (club)
rotation, noting that *"an initial delay in the uncocking of the wrist"*
allows the arm to reach greater acceleration and the club's acceleration to
be summed with the proximal segment's maximum [@milburn1982]. It is worth
pausing on the structure of that finding: the summation principle, taken
naively, prescribes *sequential initiation*; Milburn's analysis showed the
benefit comes specifically from *delaying* the distal contribution, not
merely ordering it.

Putnam's segment-interaction analyses put the principle on a dynamical
footing and simultaneously exposed its limits [@putnam1991; @putnam1993].
In a linked chain, each segment's angular acceleration depends not only on
the joint torques but on *motion-dependent interaction torques* —
centripetal and Coriolis terms proportional to the squares and products of
segment angular velocities. Putnam showed that the P→D pattern in striking
and throwing arises to a substantial degree from these interaction torques:
proximal-segment deceleration and distal-segment acceleration late in the
motion are coupled through the joint force, and they occur even without a
distal joint torque. Two implications matter for golf. First, the
kinematic order does not by itself reveal *which* torques produced it: an
identical peak sequence can be produced by different mixes of muscular and
interaction torques. Second, the deceleration of proximal segments observed
in experts need not be an active "braking" strategy — it can be, at least in
part, the dynamical *consequence* of the distal segment accelerating and
back-reacting on the chain. Marshall and Elliott further cautioned that
planar peak-ordering analyses miss long-axis rotations, which peak very late
in racquet skills and contribute substantially to end-point speed
[@marshall2000]; the golf analogue is forearm rotation and wrist action in
the final phase of the downswing.

## Double-pendulum mechanics of the golf downswing {#sec-doublependulum}

The two-lever, one-hinge model of the downswing — an "arm" link rotating
about a fixed or moving hub, connected by a wrist hinge to a "club" link —
has been the workhorse of golf mechanics since Cochran and Stobbs' *Search
for the Perfect Swing* [@cochran1968] and Jorgensen's dynamical analysis
fitted to stroboscopic photographs of a professional swing [@jorgensen1970;
@jorgensen1999]. Its enduring value for the present question is that it
makes the *timing* of the P→D handoff an explicit, controllable variable
(the "release": the point in the downswing at which the wrist angle is
allowed, or driven, to open) and exposes the mechanism by which delay pays.

Three results from this tradition anchor the analysis:

**Delayed release increases clubhead speed.** Pickering and Vickers,
sweeping release angles in a driven double-pendulum model, found clubhead
velocity at impact increases as release is delayed — the classical "late
hit" [@pickering1999]. Jorgensen's fitted model similarly reproduced the
expert swing only with a substantially delayed opening of the wrist angle
[@jorgensen1970; @jorgensen1999]. In these models an *early* release
(early P→D handoff) is strictly inferior: club kinetic energy purchased
early is paid for with arm speed that never develops.

**Late wrist torque helps; early wrist torque is the wrong tool.**
Sprigings and Neal, using a torque-driven three-segment model with
physiologically bounded actuators, found that an active wrist torque applied
*during the latter stages of the downswing* increased clubhead speed by
approximately 4% [@sprigings2000]; Sprigings and MacKenzie confirmed the
delayed-release benefit in a follow-up simulation focused specifically on
the timing of release [@sprigings2002]. The point is not that distal effort
is useless, but that its productive window is late.

**Energy transfer to the club can be largely passive — and is governed by
the changing geometry.** White analyzed an *undriven* double pendulum and
showed that the transfer of kinetic energy from arms to club late in the
downswing is a parametric-transfer phenomenon: as the club swings out, the
effective moment of inertia of the system changes, and conservation of
energy and angular momentum move kinetic energy distally without any wrist
torque at all [@white2006]. The efficiency of this transfer is controlled
principally by the wrist-cock angle maintained before release
[@white2006]. Miura's analysis of the "inward pull" complements this: an
expert's hands moving toward the body near impact — equivalent to shrinking
the hub radius when centrifugal loading is fully developed — performs work
against the centrifugal force that appears as additional clubhead kinetic
energy [@miura2001]. Nesbit and McGinnis' hub-path analyses generalize the
same idea: the non-circular hand path of skilled golfers, including its
late-downswing tightening, is a mechanism for shaping kinetic transfer from
golfer to club [@nesbit2009hub; @nesbit2014hub].

Together these results describe a machine whose highest-output operating
mode is: *load the proximal rotation first, hold the distal joint folded
(retaining the system's energy in a compact, fast-rotating configuration),
then let geometry and — in the last phase — modest distal torque move the
energy outward rapidly*. In the vocabulary of this article, the
double-pendulum literature is already an argument for **retain-early /
release-late**.

## Optimal control and torque sequencing {#sec-optimalcontrol}

If the timing question is posed as an optimization — what torque program
maximizes clubhead speed (or carry) subject to actuator limits? — the
answer has been studied repeatedly. Lampsa's early optimal-control study of
a driven double pendulum computed torque histories maximizing drive
distance, and notably found the *optimal* torques differed in structure
from those measured (via inverse dynamics) in his own swing
[@lampsa1975] — early evidence that human swings need not be optimal and
that the optimum is a meaningful target rather than a redescription of
expert behavior. Sharp, fitting shoulder-arm-club models to expert
swing data and then optimizing torque programs, established a pattern for
the best use of the available driving torques across the downswing phases,
with the distal contribution structured late rather than distributed evenly
[@sharp2009]. Three-dimensional forward-dynamics models extended the
approach with anatomically meaningful actuators and flexible shafts:
MacKenzie and Sprigings' 3D model [@mackenzie2009], the carry-optimized
model of Balzerson, Banerjee and McPhee [@balzerson2016], and the
six-degree-of-freedom dynamic optimization of McNally and McPhee
[@mcnally2018] all generate expert-like clubhead speeds with torque
programs whose distal elements act late in the downswing. McPhee's review
surveys this modeling lineage [@mcphee2022].

A caution applies in the other direction as well: the optimal-control
literature optimizes *within a model*, and the sensitivity of the optimal
timing to model structure (hub mobility, shaft flexibility, actuator
rate limits) is exactly why a multi-engine platform with cross-engine
validation (see @sec-repo) is the right instrument for revisiting the
question.

# What "energy transfer" means operationally {#sec-energyflow}

Claims about energy transfer require an accounting framework. Four levels
of analysis appear in the literature, and they are not interchangeable.

## Joint power and work

For a joint spanning segments $i$ and $i{+}1$ with net joint torque
$\tau$ and relative angular velocity $\omega$, the *joint (moment) power*
is $P_m = \tau\,\omega$; its time integral over a phase is the mechanical
work done by the net moment. Positive work indicates generation (or
concentric action), negative work absorption. This is the quantity most
golf studies report, and it is the basis of the work-power budget of
Nesbit and Serrano (@sec-workbudget) [@nesbit2005work].

## Joint-force power and segmental energy accounting {#sec-rw}

Joint moments are not the only conduit of mechanical energy: the joint
reaction force $\mathbf{F}$ acting at a joint moving with velocity
$\mathbf{v}$ transmits *joint-force power* $P_f = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{v}$
from one segment to the next. Robertson and Winter's classic formulation
balances, for each segment, the rate of change of segment mechanical energy
against the sum of joint-force powers and moment powers at its proximal and
distal ends, distinguishing energy *transferred between* segments from
energy *generated or absorbed* at joints [@robertson1980]. This is the
correct level of analysis for the question posed here, because the
"retain-early / release-late" hypothesis is precisely a claim about the
*time course of inter-segment transfer terms*, not about peak angular
velocities. As @sec-repo-gaps notes, this accounting is the principal
measurement gap in the UpstreamDrift Python stack today (the MATLAB
pipeline's per-joint linear-plus-angular work decomposition is its closest
existing realization).

## Induced accelerations and dynamic coupling

In a coupled chain, any single torque induces accelerations at *every*
joint — including joints it does not span — through the inverse inertia
matrix [@zajac1989]. Induced-acceleration and power-transfer analyses in
locomotion research [@zajac2002] show that intuitions of the form "muscle
X accelerates joint Y" routinely fail in coupled systems. For golf this
matters because a torso torque early in the downswing partly accelerates
the *club* (through coupling), and a wrist torque late in the downswing
back-reacts on the torso; the net energy routing is an emergent property
of the whole chain. The ZTCF/ZVCF decompositions of @sec-ztcf are the
counterfactual cousins of this analysis: rather than attributing
acceleration to individual torques, they split the total acceleration into
a motion-dependent (drift) part and a control part, instant by instant.

## Kinematic sequence as a proxy — and its failure modes

Peak-ordering of segment angular speeds is a *proxy* for energy flow, not a
measurement of it. Marsan and colleagues showed that the identified
kinematic sequence in golf depends materially on which angular-velocity
component (or norm, or projection) is analyzed: thirteen golfers analyzed
with seven component-selection methods yielded different sequences
[@marsan2019]. Marshall and Elliott's long-axis-rotation caution
[@marshall2000] is a special case of the same problem. Any serious test of
the timing hypothesis must therefore be run at the level of energy and
power accounting (@sec-rw), with the kinematic sequence reported as
corroborating description only.

# Empirical evidence in golfers {#sec-evidence}

## The work and power budget of the swing {#sec-workbudget}

Nesbit's full-body kinematic-kinetic study and the companion work-power
analysis of Nesbit and Serrano remain the most complete published energy
budgets of the golf swing [@nesbit2005kinematic; @nesbit2005work]. Using
subject-specific full-body models of four golfers of widely differing
skill, they report that the trunk complex (lumbar and thoracic spine plus
hips) contributes on the order of 68.7–72.2% of the total work of the
swing, the shoulder and arm joints 24.3–28%, and the legs only 3.3–3.8%
[@nesbit2005work]. Two further observations from the same study bear
directly on this article's question. First, power generation and clubhead
speed decreased systematically with increasing handicap. Second, the
authors' phase analysis locates the *generation* of energy predominantly in
the earlier downswing (torso-dominated) and the *conversion* into clubhead
speed late (shoulder/arm and club interface) — i.e., generation and
transfer are temporally separated, which is a precondition for the
retain-early / release-late strategy to even be possible.

The ground is the ultimate source of the external impulse. Han and
colleagues characterized golfer-ground interaction in 63 skilled golfers
and found meaningful associations between ground-interaction force and
moment parameters and maximum clubhead speed [@han2019]. Recent work has
pushed this to an explicitly energetic formulation: in thirty golfers
(fifteen professionals, fifteen high-level amateurs), foot-ground
interaction variables alone explained 35.5% of clubhead-speed variance,
rising to 75.4% when trunk sequencing and an *impulse-based energy-transfer
efficiency* measure (effectiveness of mechanical impulse transmission from
proximal segments to the club) were added; mediation analysis attributed
the dominant indirect pathway to transfer efficiency rather than to
sequencing per se [@frontiers2026footground]. That last distinction —
transfer *efficiency* mattering where sequence *order* alone does not — is
a recurring theme of the skill-level literature reviewed next.

## Kinematic-sequence evidence and skill-level differences {#sec-skill}

The descriptive P→D findings are robust in skilled populations. Tinmark
and colleagues, studying elite golfers across full and partial shots, found
a significant proximal-to-distal temporal ordering of peak speeds (pelvis →
torso → hands/club) with successive amplification of peak speed at every
level of effort, in both men and women [@tinmark2010]. Cheetham and
colleagues compared amateur recreational players with touring
professionals on transition- and downswing-phase kinematic sequence
parameters and found professionals showed higher peak-speed magnitudes and
more consistent sequencing/timing characteristics [@cheetham2008]. Zheng
and colleagues' three-dimensional comparison of professional and amateur
swings found systematic temporal and spatial differences, with amateurs
deviating progressively more from professional norms as handicap increased
[@zheng2008]. Meister and colleagues provide elite rotational benchmarks
(pelvis-thorax separation and its timing) against which amateurs can be
compared [@meister2011], and Lindsay, Mantrop and Vandervoort review the
broader catalogue of skill-level biomechanical differences [@lindsay2008].

Three refinements prevent an overly tidy reading:

1. **Sequence order is common but not universal — even among the best.**
   Kwon's laboratory and others have documented skilled golfers whose peak
   ordering deviates from the canonical pelvis-thorax-arm-club pattern, and
   recent work has examined how alternative sequence patterns among elite
   players relate to clubhead speed [@lee2026]. On-plane analyses of the
   "axle-chain" system in 66 skilled golfers found clubhead speed
   associations concentrated in specific angular-motion characteristics
   rather than in gross ordering [@madrid2020].

2. **Within-player timing differences do not straightforwardly explain shot
   quality.** Neal and colleagues, comparing well-timed and mistimed shots
   *within* highly skilled players, found no significant differences in the
   timing lags between peak angular speeds of contiguous segments
   [@neal2007] — the felt sense of "timing" apparently lives somewhere
   other than the inter-peak lags of a five-segment model.

3. **Method sensitivity.** As noted in @sec-energyflow, the identified
   sequence depends on component-selection methodology [@marsan2019], so
   cross-study comparisons of ordering statistics carry real uncertainty.

The empirical picture that survives these refinements: *skilled golfers
generate larger proximal speeds, separate transition from release more
distinctly, and transmit impulse/energy to the club more efficiently;
merely exhibiting a P→D peak order is neither unique to skill nor
sufficient for it*
[@cheetham2008; @zheng2008; @frontiers2026footground; @lee2026].

## Where the transfer occurs

Synthesizing @sec-workbudget and @sec-skill with the modeling results of
@sec-mechanics: in a skilled swing, the dominant energy *generation* occurs
in the trunk-hip complex during the first two-thirds of the downswing
[@nesbit2005work]; the dominant energy *transfer to the club* occurs in the
final phase, through the wrist interface, by a mechanism that is
substantially parametric/geometric (release of the wrist-cock under
centrifugal loading, hub-path tightening) with a modest late active wrist
contribution [@white2006; @miura2001; @sprigings2000; @nesbit2009hub].
Less-skilled players truncate exactly this separation: early release
("casting") moves energy into the club before proximal speed has peaked,
producing the lower distal peak speeds and lower transfer ratios observed
in amateur cohorts [@cheetham2008; @zheng2008; @milburn1982].

# The timing question, stated precisely {#sec-timing}

## Two strategies

Let $E_p(t)$ be the kinetic energy of the proximal subsystem (trunk and
arms, including the club moving with the arms as a folded unit) and
$E_c(t)$ the kinetic energy of the club, over a downswing $t \in [t_0,
t_{\mathrm{imp}}]$. Define the transfer functional as the inter-segment
power crossing the wrist interface (joint-force power plus moment power, in
the sense of @sec-rw), $P_{\mathrm{w}}(t)$. The two strategies are:

- **S1 (transfer early):** make $P_{\mathrm{w}}(t)$ large as soon after
  transition as possible; the club begins acquiring its final energy
  early, and the golfer continues adding energy to an already-fast club.
- **S2 (retain early, release late):** keep $P_{\mathrm{w}}(t)$ small
  during the first part of the downswing (the wrist interface transmits
  centripetal force but little power; the club rides with the arms), while
  proximal torques maximize $E_p$; then allow/drive a large
  $P_{\mathrm{w}}$ concentrated in the final phase.

The double-pendulum, delayed-release and optimal-control literatures
reviewed in @sec-mechanics uniformly favor S2 within their model classes
[@milburn1982; @pickering1999; @sprigings2000; @sprigings2002; @sharp2009;
@white2006]. The mechanistic reasons compose into a coherent account:

1. **Inertia management.** With the wrist cocked, the system's moment of
   inertia about the hub is small, so proximal torque buys angular velocity
   cheaply; releasing early raises the inertia while proximal torque is
   still trying to accelerate the system [@white2006; @jorgensen1999].
2. **Actuator physiology.** Torque-velocity limits mean the wrist's small
   muscles can only add meaningful power while wrist angular velocity is
   modest — i.e., late torque acts over a brief window but at high force
   transmission; early wrist torque squanders the window and can even
   require *negative* (restraining) torque later [@sprigings2000].
3. **Parametric transfer needs developed centrifugal loading.** The
   passive outward flow of energy at release, and the inward-pull gain, are
   both proportional to the centrifugal field established by proximal
   rotation; they are weak early and strong late [@white2006; @miura2001].
4. **Interaction torques do the late work for free.** Putnam-style
   motion-dependent torques accelerate the distal segment and decelerate
   the proximal one automatically once release begins; the golfer's job is
   to *time* this cascade, not to muscle it [@putnam1993].

Empirically, S2-like signatures separate skill groups (later release,
larger proximal speeds before release, higher transfer efficiency;
@sec-skill), while the within-expert null result on inter-peak lags
[@neal2007] suggests that once S2 is grossly achieved, the residual
performance variance lives in finer variables (release profile shape,
hub-path geometry, impulse-transfer efficiency) — exactly the variables the
counterfactual framework below is designed to expose.

## What would falsify S2?

To keep the question scientific rather than rhetorical, we state what
evidence would count against the retain-early/release-late hypothesis:

- an optimal-control solution, in a validated 3D model with physiological
  actuator limits, whose optimal wrist-interface power is front-loaded;
- measured expert swings in which early wrist-interface power (normalized)
  is *positively* associated with clubhead speed across players;
- counterfactual (ZTCF/ZVCF) analyses showing that in faster swings the
  control term dominates club acceleration *early* rather than late.

The proposed experiments of @sec-proposed-experiments operationalize these
tests.

# Counterfactual decompositions: ZTCF and ZVCF {#sec-ztcf}

## Definitions

Write the chain's equation of motion in standard manipulator form:

$$
M(q)\,\ddot q \;=\; \tau \;-\; b(q, \dot q),
\qquad
b(q,\dot q) \;=\; C(q,\dot q)\,\dot q \;+\; g(q) \;+\; d(\dot q),
$$ {#eq-eom}

with inertia matrix $M$, applied generalized torques $\tau$, Coriolis and
centripetal terms $C\dot q$, gravity $g$, and velocity-dependent
dissipation $d$. Two counterfactual accelerations are defined *pointwise*
at each measured state $(q, \dot q, \tau)$ of a swing:

$$
\ddot q_{\mathrm{ZTCF}}
  \;=\; M(q)^{-1}\,\bigl(-\,b(q,\dot q)\bigr),
$$ {#eq-ztcf}

$$
\ddot q_{\mathrm{ZVCF}}
  \;=\; M(q)^{-1}\,\bigl(\tau \;-\; b(q,\mathbf{0})\bigr)
  \;=\; M(q)^{-1}\,\bigl(\tau \;-\; g(q)\bigr),
$$ {#eq-zvcf}

where the simplification in @eq-zvcf holds because the Coriolis term
(quadratic in velocity) and viscous dissipation (linear in velocity) vanish
at $\dot q = \mathbf 0$. The ZTCF (@eq-ztcf) answers *"what would the
system do right now if every actuator switched off?"* — it is the **drift**
field of the affine control system, containing gravity plus all
motion-dependent interaction dynamics. The ZVCF (@eq-zvcf) answers *"what
would the current muscular effort produce from a standstill in this
pose?"* — it isolates the instantaneous contribution of control from the
contribution of accumulated motion. Because @eq-eom is affine in $\tau$,
the actual acceleration superposes exactly:

$$
\ddot q \;=\;
\underbrace{M^{-1}(-b(q,\dot q))}_{\text{drift}\;=\;\text{ZTCF}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{M^{-1}\tau}_{\text{control}},
$$ {#eq-superposition}

an identity enforced to numerical tolerance by the repository's test suite
(@sec-repo-validation).

## Two operational variants

The repository implements two distinct operationalizations, and the
difference matters for interpretation:

**Pointwise (instantaneous) counterfactuals.** The engine-agnostic Python
implementation
([`simulation_backends/ztcf_zvcf.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/simulation_backends/ztcf_zvcf.py))
evaluates @eq-ztcf and @eq-zvcf at each sample of an already-measured
trajectory. It is explicitly *not* a forward-integrated rollout: each
sample answers a local "what if" without propagating the hypothetical
forward. This is the right tool for constructing drift/control *time
profiles* along a real swing.

**Re-simulation counterfactuals.** The original MATLAB/Simscape pipeline
([`run_ztcf_simulation.m`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/Simscape_Multibody_Models/2D_Golf_Model/matlab_optimized/core/simulation/run_ztcf_simulation.m))
re-simulates the full model with a torque "killswitch" applied at time $t$,
for a sweep of $t$ values, tabulating the counterfactual state reached with
torques off. The pipeline forms the difference table
$\mathrm{DELTA} = \mathrm{BASE} - \mathrm{ZTCF}$
([`process_data_tables.m`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/Simscape_Multibody_Models/2D_Golf_Model/matlab_optimized/core/processing/process_data_tables.m)),
attributing to active control everything the passive system would not have
done. A companion ZVCF model applies the measured torques to the same pose
with velocities zeroed
([`SCRIPT_ZVCF_GENERATOR.m`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/Simscape_Multibody_Models/2D_Golf_Model/matlab/Model%20Output/Scripts/SCRIPT_ZVCF_GENERATOR.m));
run without gravity, the ZVCF and ZTCF contributions superpose to the BASE
motion, mirroring @eq-superposition at the level of simulated trajectories.
The MATLAB pipeline additionally computes, for every joint and every table
(BASE, ZTCF, DELTA), the linear work $\int \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt$,
angular work $\int \boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\,dt$, total work
and power, and the fractional contributions ZTCF/BASE and DELTA/BASE
([`calculate_work_impulse.m`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/Simscape_Multibody_Models/2D_Golf_Model/matlab_optimized/core/processing/calculate_work_impulse.m),
[`calculate_total_work_power.m`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/Simscape_Multibody_Models/2D_Golf_Model/matlab_optimized/core/processing/calculate_total_work_power.m))
— precisely the Robertson-Winter-style joint-interface accounting
(@sec-rw) that the timing question needs, including a kinematic-sequence
plot computed *separately for the BASE, ZTCF and DELTA components*
([`SCRIPT_324_PLOT_ZTCF_KinematicSequence.m`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/Simscape_Multibody_Models/2D_Golf_Model/matlab/Scripts/_ZTCF%20Scripts/SCRIPT_324_PLOT_ZTCF_KinematicSequence.m)).

## The counterfactual form of the timing hypothesis

The ZTCF/ZVCF language makes the S2 hypothesis crisp. Along a measured
downswing, project the drift and control accelerations onto the club's
speed-producing direction and integrate the associated powers. S2 predicts,
for high-performing swings:

- **Early downswing:** the *control* term should dominate energy input at
  proximal joints, while at the wrist interface the control contribution to
  club angular acceleration should be small or even negative (restraining
  lag against the developing centrifugal field). The ZTCF profile of the
  club should show that, had torques been removed, the club would have
  released outward — i.e., the drift field already "wants" to open the
  wrist, and control is *holding energy back*.
- **Late downswing:** the *drift* term (interaction dynamics: parametric
  transfer, centrifugal release) should dominate club acceleration, with a
  brief late window of positive wrist control power [@sprigings2000]. The
  DELTA (active) share of club-side work should be concentrated before
  release; the ZTCF (passive) share should account for most club energy
  gain after release [@white2006].

This is the pattern the repository's preliminary MATLAB analyses motivated,
and it is stated here as a *hypothesis to be quantified*, not a result: the
figures and tables that would substantiate it are the deliverable of issue
[#8377](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/issues/8377).
Conversely, if high-performing swings show early-dominant wrist control
power, S2 is falsified in exactly the terms of @sec-timing.

This section inventories the repository's relevant capabilities, so that
the proposed experiments can be read against what exists. Links point to
the `main` branch.

## Counterfactual stack

The normative contract lives in the engine-core dynamics interface
([`_dynamics_interface.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/engine_core/_dynamics_interface.py)):
`compute_drift_acceleration`, `compute_control_acceleration`,
`compute_ztcf`, `compute_zvcf`, with the superposition identity
(@eq-superposition) stated as a contract. Engine implementations exist for
MuJoCo, Drake, Pinocchio, OpenSim, MyoSuite, the analytic pendulum engines,
and the Simscape bridge; the capability matrix is documented in
[`engine_capabilities.md`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/docs/engines/engine_capabilities.md).
On top of these sit:

- the pointwise engine-agnostic evaluator with HDF5 persistence
  ([`ztcf_zvcf.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/simulation_backends/ztcf_zvcf.py));
- a MuJoCo delta-based counterfactual analyzer reporting
  torque-attributed and velocity-attributed acceleration effects
  ([`counterfactuals.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/physics_engines/mujoco/python/mujoco_humanoid_golf/counterfactuals.py));
- a Newton-Euler ZTCF force module with an analytic single-pendulum
  validation identity
  ([`biomechanics/ztcf.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/biomechanics/ztcf.py));
- induced-acceleration analyzers (gravity / drift / control / total
  components)
  ([`induced_acceleration.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/physics_engines/mujoco/python/mujoco_humanoid_golf/rigid_body_dynamics/induced_acceleration.py));
- an orchestration layer with capability gating and a REST/UI surface
  ([`analysis/orchestrator.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/analysis/orchestrator.py));
- the MATLAB re-simulation pipeline described in @sec-ztcf.

## Energy and power computations

- **Inter-segment power flow (MuJoCo):**
  [`power_flow.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/engines/physics_engines/mujoco/python/mujoco_humanoid_golf/power_flow.py)
  computes per-DOF joint powers $\tau\omega$, work decomposed into drift
  and control shares, per-body kinetic and potential energies via
  center-of-mass Jacobians, per-body parent/child transfer bookkeeping, and
  an energy-conservation residual derived from the equations of motion.
- **Joint work/power/impulse metrics (engine-agnostic):**
  [`power_work_metrics.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/analysis/power_work_metrics.py)
  (positive/negative/net work, generation-absorption splits, impulse,
  quasi-stiffness);
  [`energy_metrics.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/analysis/energy_metrics.py)
  (system energy summaries).
- **Conservation monitoring:**
  [`energy_monitor.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/physics/energy_monitor.py)
  enforces drift bounds on total energy during integration (note: its
  potential-energy term is a documented first-order approximation, adequate
  for drift detection only).
- **MATLAB energetics:** the per-joint linear/angular work and power
  decomposition across BASE/ZTCF/DELTA tables (@sec-ztcf) — currently the
  richest joint-interface energy accounting in the repository.

## Sequencing analytics

- [`kinematic_sequence.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/biomechanics/kinematic_sequence.py):
  peak detection, ordering consistency against a caller-supplied expected
  order, timing gaps, distal/proximal speed-gain ratios, post-peak
  deceleration rates. (Deliberately method-neutral; the expected order is
  user-defined.)
- [`coordination_metrics.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/analysis/coordination_metrics.py):
  vector-coding coupling angles, continuous relative phase, pairwise lag
  matrices — quantitative sequencing measures less brittle than
  peak-ordering.
- Plot renderers for sequence traces, peak-timing Gantt charts, and lag
  matrices
  ([`_coordination_sequence.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/src/shared/python/plotting/renderers/_coordination_sequence.py)).
- An approved internal research review of the kinematic-sequence metric,
  including literature benchmarks and uncertainty-reporting guidance
  ([`kinematic_sequence.md`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/docs/assessments/research_reviews/kinematic_sequence.md)).

## Validation evidence {#sec-repo-validation}

The counterfactual stack is contract-tested: ZTCF/ZVCF from independent
backends agree with analytic ground truth to $10^{-9}$
([`test_ztcf_zvcf.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/tests/unit/simulation_backends/test_ztcf_zvcf.py));
drift-plus-control reconstructs the measured acceleration
([`test_counterfactual_experiments.py`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/tests/acceptance/test_counterfactual_experiments.py));
work-energy-theorem and conservation-law property tests run in CI
([`tests/integration/conservation_laws/`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/tree/main/tests/integration/conservation_laws));
and a cross-engine comparison service produces divergence-annotated
ZTCF/ZVCF panels between backends
([`cross_engine_comparison.md`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/docs/simulation_backends/cross_engine_comparison.md)).
The project's design guidelines make the drift-control decomposition and
ZTCF/ZVCF availability normative across engines
([`project_design_guidelines.qmd`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/main/docs/project_design_guidelines.qmd)).

## Gaps relevant to this article {#sec-repo-gaps}

| Gap | Consequence for the timing question |
|---|---|
| Two ZTCF operationalizations (pointwise vs re-simulation) coexist; no Python re-simulation ZTCF | Analyses must state which variant they use; parity between variants is untested |
| Inter-segment power transfer implemented only for MuJoCo, as joint power $\tau\omega$ | Wrist-interface *force* power $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf v$ — central to S1/S2 — is not yet computed in Python |
| No Robertson-Winter segmental energy-flow accounting in Python | The transfer functional $P_{\mathrm w}(t)$ must currently come from the MATLAB tables |
| `ConservationMonitor` potential energy is first-order approximate | Do not report absolute PE from it; use engine energy accessors |
| Flexible-shaft strain energy absent from the energy budget | Late-downswing shaft recoil energy is invisible to current accounting |
| Proximal-braking-efficiency metric is an open TODO | Deceleration-side claims must rely on generic post-peak deceleration rates |

: Known gaps (tracked in issue [#8378](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/issues/8378)). {#tbl-gaps}

# Synthesis: early or late? {#sec-synthesis}

**What is established.** (i) Skilled golf swings exhibit P→D ordering with
successive speed amplification, robustly across shot types and populations
[@tinmark2010; @cheetham2008]. (ii) The trunk-hip complex does most of the
work; the club acquires most of its energy late, through the wrist
interface [@nesbit2005work; @nesbit2005kinematic]. (iii) In every
published double-pendulum, delayed-release, and optimal-control analysis,
delaying the distal handoff increases clubhead speed, and productive distal
torque is late [@milburn1982; @pickering1999; @sprigings2000;
@sprigings2002; @sharp2009]. (iv) The late transfer is substantially
passive — parametric/geometric — once proximal rotation has established the
centrifugal field [@white2006; @miura2001]. (v) Skill differences appear
in magnitudes, transition timing, and transfer efficiency more than in
gross order [@cheetham2008; @zheng2008; @frontiers2026footground].

**What this implies for the question.** The weight of evidence supports
**S2: retain energy proximally early in the downswing and accelerate the
transfer late.** The phrase "retain energy proximally" deserves precision:
it does not mean suppressing proximal motion — proximal segments should be
accelerated as hard as the movement budget allows — it means *deferring the
handoff*: keeping the wrist interface transmitting force but little power
(club folded, riding with the arms) until late, so that the energy pool is
large and the centrifugal field strong when the parametric transfer is
allowed to run. In counterfactual terms: early control effort should
appear at proximal joints and, at the wrist, partly as *restraint* of the
drift field's tendency to release; late club energy gain should be
drift-dominated with a brief late window of positive wrist control power
(@sec-ztcf).

**What remains genuinely open.** (a) The published S2 evidence is
model-based or observational; a *direct* energetic accounting of the wrist
interface across skill levels (the $P_{\mathrm w}(t)$ time course) has not
been reported in the literature reviewed here — the closest is the
impulse-transfer-efficiency result of [@frontiers2026footground], which is
consistent with, but does not resolve, the timing profile. (b) Optimal
timing is plausibly equipment- and anthropometry-dependent (shaft
flexibility, club MOI, segment lengths), and model sensitivity is untested
across engines. (c) Whether *actively* restraining release (negative wrist
torque early) outperforms merely *not driving* release is unresolved in
3D models with realistic actuators — Jorgensen's and White's analyses
suggest passive holding suffices in 2D [@jorgensen1999; @white2006], while
Sprigings-Neal-type actuator models leave room for an active-restraint
benefit [@sprigings2000]. These are precisely the questions the
repository's toolchain can answer.

# Proposed experiments {#sec-proposed-experiments}

The following designs are specified so that each has a pre-registered,
falsifiable outcome measure. They are tracked in issue
[#8377](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/issues/8377); no
results exist yet, and none are reported here.

**E1 — Torque-timing sweep (double pendulum and 8-DOF golfer).** Drive
the models of @tbl-models with parameterized torque programs: proximal
torque fixed; wrist torque onset time $t_{\mathrm{on}}$, sign profile
(restrain-then-drive vs drive-only), and magnitude swept on a grid; impact
defined by club alignment. Outcome: clubhead speed at impact as a function
of $t_{\mathrm{on}}$ and profile. S2 predicts a late-interior optimum of
$t_{\mathrm{on}}$ and a non-inferior or superior restrain-then-drive
profile. The MJX/Warp batched backends make the sweep cheap; the ODE
backend provides the reference.

**E2 — Counterfactual energy budget along swept trajectories.** For each
E1 trajectory, evaluate the pointwise ZTCF/ZVCF and drift/control split
(@eq-superposition) and integrate drift-side and control-side club power.
Outcome: the fraction of final club kinetic energy attributable to drift
vs control in early vs late downswing halves, as a function of performance.
S2 predicts the drift share of late club energy gain rises with clubhead
speed across the sweep.

**E3 — Re-simulation parity.** Implement the killswitch re-simulation
ZTCF in Python on the backend-neutral model; compare against both the
pointwise ZTCF profiles and the MATLAB pipeline on matched trajectories
(cross-engine comparison service). Outcome: documented agreement/divergence
between the two ZTCF operationalizations, closing the top gap of
@tbl-gaps.

**E4 — Wrist-interface power accounting.** Implement Robertson-Winter
segmental energy flow (joint force power $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$ plus
moment power $\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega$ at each interface;
issue [#8378](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/issues/8378)),
then compute $P_{\mathrm w}(t)$ for E1's best and worst performers.
Outcome: the direct time course of the transfer functional that
@sec-timing defines — the primary evidence either strategy needs.

**E5 — Mocap replication.** Run the E2/E4 analyses on measured swings
ingested through the repository's motion pipeline (C3D → tracked motion),
across available skill levels. Outcome: observational test of the
counterfactual predictions of @sec-ztcf against human data, with the
uncertainty-reporting conventions of the internal research review.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

This article synthesizes literature and specifies methodology; it reports
no new data, and the S2 hypothesis, while strongly supported by the
modeling literature, remains unquantified in the repository's own terms
until the experiments of @sec-proposed-experiments are executed. The
kinematic-sequence evidence base carries known methodological sensitivity
[@marsan2019]; several classical results rest on planar models whose
generalization to 3D swings with mobile hubs is a live modeling question
[@mcphee2022]; and the work-budget percentages cited from
[@nesbit2005work] derive from four subjects. One recent source
[@frontiers2026footground] is cited without its author list because the
publisher's site was unreachable through this environment's network proxy
at the time of writing; readers should resolve the DOI for full
bibliographic details. Finally, energy-based arguments here concern
clubhead *speed*; accuracy, consistency, and injury-risk trade-offs of
late-transfer strategies [@hume2005; @lindsay2008] are outside scope.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

Proximal-to-distal sequencing in the golf swing is real, robust, and — as
a coaching target — chronically over-interpreted. The mechanical
literature, from Cochran and Stobbs through modern optimal control, does
not support "pass the energy along as soon as possible." It supports a
subtler program: *build the energy proximally with the club held folded,
defer the handoff, and let the transfer run — mostly parametrically, with a
brief late assist — when the centrifugal field can pay for it*. Skilled
players differ from amateurs precisely along this axis: not in whether
their segments peak in order, but in how much energy the proximal system
holds at transition, how late and how efficiently it is handed to the club.
The ZTCF/ZVCF counterfactual framework implemented in UpstreamDrift turns
this qualitative account into measurable time profiles — drift versus
control, passive versus active, early versus late — and the experiment
suite specified here (epic
[#8373](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/issues/8373))
is designed to either quantify the retain-early/release-late advantage or
falsify it. Either outcome would be a contribution.
